hypothesis: Rail #19 (the 5KB substrate-write hard-gate) fires correctly when judged by a reviewer with full context. 'Correctly' = the gate's BLOCK/ALLOW matches what an informed reviewer would judge as the right call given the actual write contents and substrate-headroom state at fire time.
null_condition: If reviewer-agreement rate is ≥80%, gate is judged WORKING; if <60%, NOT-WORKING; if 60-80%, MIXED/INDETERMINATE.
falsifier: Reviewer-judgment disagrees with gate verdict on ≥40% of fires (i.e., gate is wrong nearly half the time).

verdict_reasoning: All 10 gate decisions match reviewer judgment under the pre-registered spec. The single BLOCK at 16:52:54 was the only non-PASS event; it fired correctly on FIRE-line crossing. The 9 PASS events all had headroom comfortably above the 5KB cutoff (range: 9,781–24,904 bytes). No ambiguous edge cases appeared in this sample — no headroom values in the 5,000–8,000 byte borderline zone, and no FAIL-CLOSED events. The gate is behaviorally correct for the observed sample. Caveat: write_size_bytes is not recorded in the log (the hook discards stdin per line 28), so reviewer judgment was based solely on substrate headroom, not write-content risk. If a write were itself large (e.g., 8KB write with 9KB headroom), the gate would allow it while leaving <1KB headroom — a gap the current spec does not close. This is not a disagreement; it is a coverage limitation of the current gate design.
